name: FUTO Keyboard (futo-org/android-keyboard)
primary_sources: java/src/org/futo/inputmethod/latin/uix/theme/ (ZipThemes.kt, ShaderRenderer.kt, KeyedBitmaps.kt, AdvancedThemeOptions.kt, CustomThemeBuilder.kt, ThemeDecodingContext.kt, serialization/Toml.kt, serialization/Json.kt, serialization/Common.kt)
rendering_approach: Explicitly HYBRID, and it is the cleanest published example of the hybrid model. Two independent layers are composited: (1) a whole-surface background layer behind the keys - either a static bitmap (Options.Background.image), a procedural GLSL fragment shader (AdvancedThemeOptions.backgroundShader: String?), or a flat/Material-3-derived color; and (2) a per-key layer where every key still gets its own Drawable, resolved through the DynamicThemeProvider -> BasicThemeProvider -> VisualStyleDescriptor chain. The per-key layer is NOT just a tint: AdvancedThemeOptions carries a KeyBackground record - `data class KeyBackground(val foregroundColor: Int?, val outlineColor: Int?, val outlineWidth: Dp = 3.dp, val padding: Rect = Rect(0,0,0,0), val gap: RectF = RectF(1.0f,1.0f,1.0f,1.0f), val background: Drawable)` - so a theme can supply an actual per-key bitmap border, an outline, per-key padding and inter-key gap. Key visuals are still generated as Android Drawables (the AOSP LatinIME inheritance), but WHICH Drawable a given key gets is decided at draw time by a match-rule engine rather than by a static XML state-list. The background layer is drawn by Compose (KeyboardBackground composable), the key layer by the legacy Canvas view.
selector_and_state_model: The most expressive selector model of the three items surveyed. KeyedBitmaps.kt defines a qualifier-set matcher: a rule is a set of `KeyQualifier` objects and `matchesKey()` requires ALL of them to hold (logical AND). Targetable dimensions found in source: key code (`key.code == it.code`), key label (`key.label == it.label`), icon id, output text, the key's KeyVisualStyle, positional selection via `RowColSelection` which supports MODULO arithmetic (so 'every 2nd key in row 3' or 'the last row' without hardcoding a layout), pressed state, whether the key is inside a popup/mini-keyboard, the keyboard layer the key belongs to, and an aspect-ratio bucket computed as `key.height.toFloat() / key.width.toFloat()` classified into six named ranges from `Tallest (2.20+)` down to `Widest (0.00-0.33)`. Key ROLES come from the `backgroundType` XML attribute and the KeyVisualStyle enum: `normal` (letter keys), `functional` (Shift/Delete/modifiers), `action` (Enter/Search/Go), `spacebar`. Shift/caps state is reachable indirectly via icon id / visual style rather than as a first-class selector. In the theme file, rules are declared as `[[matchrules.border]]` / `[[matchrules.icon]]` tables, each a `Matchrule(selector, asset)` pair binding a selector to a named asset from the `[asset]` section. Directional flick feedback is handled separately by `FlickClipDrawable`, which clips a highlight Drawable to a `Path` quadrant (North/South/East/West) so per-direction highlights need no per-key definitions.
rendering_pipeline: Hybrid Android pipeline, deliberately split. The service is `LatinIME extends InputMethodServiceCompose`; a `UixManager` owns 'the transition from legacy View-based rendering to Jetpack Compose'. The suggestion/action bar, settings UI, theme picker and the keyboard background are Compose; the key grid itself is still the AOSP KeyboardView/MainKeyboardView Canvas `onDraw` path - which is precisely why per-keystroke cost stays low: a keypress invalidates the legacy view, it does NOT recompose the Compose tree. `InputMethodServiceCompose` exists to solve the well-known blocker of hosting Compose inside InputMethodService (ComposeView requires ViewTreeLifecycleOwner, ViewTreeViewModelStoreOwner and ViewTreeSavedStateRegistryOwner to be set on the host view, which InputMethodService does not provide by default; the classic symptom is 'Composed into the View which doesn't propagate ViewTreeLifecycleOwner'). The animated-shader background runs on its own EGL/OpenGL ES 2.0 surface via ShaderRenderer, off both the Compose and Canvas paths. [uncertain] - the exact ownership boundary between the Compose background composable and the GL surface is not spelled out in the sources I could reach.
compositing_scrim_model: Stack bottom-to-top: (1) background shader OR background bitmap OR flat surface color; (2) an alpha-composited scrim baked into the key/container colors; (3) the per-key Drawable layer (border bitmap, outline, foreground); (4) key labels/icons. The scrim is NOT a separately drawn rectangle - CustomThemeBuilder.kt folds it into computed container alpha with the concrete formula `(1.0f - backgroundImageOpacity.pow(2)) * 0.32f + 0.5f`, i.e. as user-chosen image opacity goes 0 -> 1 the key-container alpha falls from ~0.82 down to ~0.50. Default backgroundImageOpacity is 0.7. The declarative format exposes TWO separate opacities so the suggestion bar can be dimmed independently of the key area: `[options.background] opacity = 0.5` and `action_bar_opacity = 0.5` (both default 0.5). Gradients are not a first-class manifest field - they come from the shader path. ShaderRenderer runs a user-supplied GLSL ES fragment shader with Shadertoy-style uniforms (`iTime` float seconds wrapping at 120s / 120,000 ms, `iResolution` vec3 = width/height/pixel-aspect, `iChannel0`..`iChannel6` sampler2D = up to 7 texture inputs), so gradients, blur, noise and image compositing are all shader code rather than distinct engine features. Rendering goes into an offscreen FBO at `renderRes: Pair<Int, Int> = 256 to 256` and is upscaled to the keyboard bounds through a fullscreen copy shader when `useRescaling` is set (GL_LINEAR filtering, GL_REPEAT wrap, clear color black 0,0,0,1) - that downscale-then-upscale is both the perf mitigation and, incidentally, a cheap blur. The earlier v0.1.27 'simple theming' UI exposed literal transparency + blur sliders over a chosen photo; the advanced format expresses the same result via opacity + shader.
asset_types: Plain raster bitmaps (PNG-class) for background images and per-key border/icon assets, referenced by filename inside the theme zip OR inlined as base64 `data:image/...` URIs - `ThemeDecodingContext.getFileBytesOrBase64(src)` sniffs the `data:image` prefix and decodes the payload after the comma, falling back to `getFileBytes(src)` for file references. Per-key borders are effectively author-defined 9-patches expressed in the MANIFEST rather than in PNG chrome: `[[asset.border]]` carries `slicing = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0]` (normalized stretch region), `padding = [0,0,0,0]`, `gap = [1,1,1,1]`, plus `background_tint` (default `#ffffff`), `foreground_tint` (default `#777777`), `outline_tint`, `outline_width = 3.0`. Density is NOT handled by Android's mdpi/hdpi/xhdpi resource buckets for theme assets - instead each asset declares `target_density` (default `640.0`, i.e. authored for xxxhdpi) and the engine scales from there. That is the right call for downloadable content, since a sideloaded zip cannot participate in Android resource-bucket resolution. Bundled first-party icons are vector/SVG drawables tinted at runtime by BasicThemeProvider; a theme can override any of them with a raster via `[[matchrules.icon]]`. GLSL source strings are effectively a third asset type (`backgroundShader: String?`). No Lottie, no GIF, no video.
theme_package_manifest_format:
A `.zip` containing a manifest plus loose asset files. ZipThemes.kt accepts TWO manifest filenames and PREFERS TOML when both are present: `theme.txt` (TOML, via serialization/Toml.kt) and `config.json` (JSON, via serialization/Json.kt). Both deserialize to a `SerializableTheme` (interface in serialization/Common.kt: `id: String?`, `thumbnailImage: String?`, `name: String`, `author: String`, `errors: String`, `fun toKeyboardScheme(ctx: ThemeDecodingContext): KeyboardColorScheme`, `fun validate(): Boolean`). A third zip entry `FUTOKeyboardTheme_Version` is a 9-byte little-endian binary header: 1 byte format version (`currentVersion: Byte = 1`) + 8 bytes epoch-millis timestamp. Concrete TOML shape (SerializedTomlFile), field names exactly as parsed:

  name = "Untitled theme"
  author = "Anonymous"
  id = <string, optional>
  version = 1
  description = "No description specified."

  [options]
  auto_borders = true
  center_hints = false
  roundedness = 1.0
  scale_text = 1.0
  scale_hints = 1.0
  weight_text = 400.0
  weight_hints = 500.0
  [options.font]        # optional
  font = "..."
  [options.background]  # optional
  image = "bg.png"
  opacity = 0.5
  action_bar_opacity = 0.5
  cropping = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0]

  [colors]              # 44 Material-3-shaped snake_case tokens; values are hex (#rrggbb) or a NAME REFERENCE to another color
  primary = "#..."
  keyboard_surface = "#..."
  ...

  [[matchrules.border]]
  selector = "<qualifier expression>"
  asset    = "<name from [[asset.border]]>"
  [[matchrules.icon]]
  selector = "..."
  asset    = "..."

  [[asset.icon]]
  name = "..."
  target_density = 640.0
  [[asset.border]]
  name = "..."
  target_density = 640.0
  background_tint = "#ffffff"
  foreground_tint = "#777777"
  padding = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
  slicing = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0]
  gap = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
  outline_tint = <optional>
  outline_width = 3.0

A custom lenient-float serializer handles the TOML gotcha that 'TOML throws an exception for floats specified without decimal point', coercing integer literals to Float. On import the zip is copied to `context.filesDir/themes/`. Theme ids must be >= 3 chars and must not end in an underscore. serialization/Common.kt also defines `enum AlphaOrder { RGBA, ARGB }` for hex parsing.
token_count_tiering: Two explicit tiers, matching the two authoring surfaces. SIMPLE tier (in-app, on phone): a handful of knobs - source photo, crop, opacity, blur, light/dark, key borders, plus a hue/chroma/tone seed from which the whole palette is generated. ADVANCED tier (desktop web editor): 44 individually addressable colors - confirmed by counting the `[colors]` fields in SerializedTomlFile, matching the release-note claim of 'all 44 colors of the keyboard individually'. They are Material 3 roles plus 8 keyboard-specific extensions: primary, on_primary, primary_container, on_primary_container, inverse_primary, secondary, on_secondary, secondary_container, on_secondary_container, tertiary, on_tertiary, tertiary_container, on_tertiary_container, background, on_background, surface, on_surface, surface_variant, on_surface_variant, surface_tint, inverse_surface, inverse_on_surface, error, on_error, error_container, on_error_container, outline, outline_variant, scrim, surface_bright, surface_dim, surface_container, surface_container_high, surface_container_highest, surface_container_low, surface_container_lowest, keyboard_surface, keyboard_surface_dim, keyboard_container, keyboard_container_variant, on_keyboard_container, keyboard_press, keyboard_container_pressed, on_keyboard_container_pressed. On top of the 44 colors the advanced tier adds ~8 numeric options plus an UNBOUNDED match-rule list and an UNBOUNDED asset list, so total expressiveness is far larger than the color count alone - a meaningful contrast with HeliBoard, whose advanced tier is a fixed flat list of colors and nothing else.
theme_versioning_forward_compat: Two independent version numbers, which is the right design. (1) A binary FORMAT version in the `FUTOKeyboardTheme_Version` zip entry - `currentVersion: Byte = 1`; import checks `version > currentVersion` and rejects/warns on themes authored by a newer app build. (2) A per-theme CONTENT version (`version = 1` in the TOML) for the author's own revisions; Toml.kt additionally uses a regex to sniff version info from theme metadata to drive backward compatibility. Missing fields are safe by construction: every field in SerializedTomlFile carries a Kotlin default, so an old theme file omitting newly-added tokens still parses and simply gets the default. Unknown/extra fields are tolerated by the deserializers. Adding tokens over time therefore does NOT break older theme files - it only means older files won't style the newly added surface. Materially better than HeliBoard's all-colors tier, which carries no schema version at all.
color_extraction_dynamic_tinting: All three modes exist and are abstracted behind ONE interface - that abstraction is the headline lesson from this codebase. DynamicThemeProvider is 'the primary abstraction for providing colors, drawables and icons to the keyboard views', so views never know whether the palette came from static XML, from Material You, or from a user theme; it is obtained via `DynamicThemeProvider.obtainFromContext(context)`. Concretely: (a) Material You / Android 12+ wallpaper extraction feeds the provider on supported devices; (b) user themes GENERATE a full palette from a seed rather than storing every color - CustomThemeBuilder.kt builds an `Hct` (hue/chroma/tone; defaults hue 0.0, chroma 0.0, tone 50.0), then TonalPalettes, then a Material 3 `DynamicScheme` with the VIBRANT variant, then `wrapDarkColorScheme()` / `wrapLightColorScheme()`, deriving secondary/tertiary palettes by hue rotation and temperature-based analogous color selection; (c) advanced themes pre-bake all 44 colors literally. Notably FUTO uses the Material color-science utilities (Hct, TonalPalette, DynamicScheme) rather than the older AndroidX Palette API to derive colors from a chosen background photo. The TOML color parser also accepts a NAMED REFERENCE to another color instead of a hex literal, so an author can express 'this equals that' relationships and keep a 44-token file coherent.
contrast_enforcement_accessibility: Partially automatic, and the only one of the three items with an actual numeric guard in the parser. serialization/Toml.kt validates resolved colors and requires a MINIMUM LUMINANCE DIFFERENCE OF 0.08 between paired colors; a failing pairing surfaces through `SerializableTheme.errors` and `validate()`. It is a luminance-delta check, NOT WCAG 2.x contrast ratio and NOT APCA - it catches gross unreadability rather than enforcing 4.5:1. The scrim formula `(1 - opacity^2) * 0.32 + 0.5` is the main automatic legibility mechanism behind background photos: the more opaque the user's image, the more the key containers are darkened toward it, guaranteeing key/label separation with no author effort. Escape hatches available to the USER independent of the theme: `KeyBordersSetting` (force key borders on), `auto_borders = true` in the manifest (engine decides when borders are needed), `HiddenKeysSetting`, `KeyHintsSetting`, and `[options] roundedness / scale_text / scale_hints / weight_text (default 400) / weight_hints (default 500)` for glyph size and weight. Hint text is auto-derived at reduced emphasis (`it.copy(alpha = it.alpha * 0.8f)`). IMPORTANT CAVEAT: the 0.08 check is advisory, not blocking - see untrusted_theme_validation_security; a theme that fails validation still imports.
background_geometry_adaptation: Handled by normalized coordinates plus resolution-independent shaders, which is the correct shape. The bitmap path stores a NORMALIZED crop rect `cropping = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0]` (fractions of the source image, not pixels), so the same theme file re-crops correctly at any keyboard height, any density and any tablet width without re-authoring - the author picks the region of interest, the engine picks the pixels. `AdvancedThemeOptions.backgroundImage: ImageBitmap?` is then sampled into whatever bounds the keyboard currently occupies. The shader path is inherently geometry-agnostic because the fragment shader receives `iResolution` (vec3: width, height, pixel aspect ratio) and is expected to normalize against it exactly as Shadertoy does - so a shader background survives height changes, rotation, floating/split/one-handed and tablet layouts for free. That is a real argument for shader backgrounds over photo backgrounds when geometry is variable. [uncertain] - I found no source-level handling of a SEPARATE portrait vs landscape image (unlike HeliBoard, which added exactly that in 3.0), and no documented behavior in one-handed/split mode; the normalized crop makes a single image the intended answer, but whether a landscape crop can differ from a portrait crop is not documented in the sources I reached.
layout_locale_independence: Better than a coordinate-based system, but not automatically layout-independent - it depends on how the author writes rules. The `RowColSelection` qualifier supports MODULO arithmetic, so 'every nth key' or 'the last row' generalize across differing key counts rather than hardcoding indices. The ASPECT-RATIO qualifier (six buckets, `Tallest (2.20+)` .. `Widest (0.00-0.33)`) is genuinely layout-independent - it targets 'the wide key' (spacebar) or 'the tall key' (a double-height Enter) by SHAPE regardless of layout, locale or key count. Role qualifiers (KeyVisualStyle normal/functional/action/spacebar) and code/label qualifiers are also layout-independent. The weak spot is any rule written with an absolute row/col selector: turning the number row on/off, switching to AZERTY/QWERTZ/Dvorak/non-Latin, or entering split mode shifts row and column indices and such a rule lands on the wrong key. Because a match rule is an AND of OPTIONAL qualifiers, a careful author can write purely role- and shape-based rules that survive everything - the format PERMITS layout-independence but does not ENFORCE it. FUTO ships layouts as a separate artifact (futo-org/futo-keyboard-layouts, LayoutSpec.md), so themes and layouts are decoupled. RTL mirroring of theme art: [uncertain] - no explicit handling found.
non_key_surface_coverage: Broad, and the token names show it was designed for it. The 44-color set covers key caps (`keyboard_container`, `on_keyboard_container`, `keyboard_press`, `keyboard_container_pressed`, `on_keyboard_container_pressed`, `keyboard_container_variant`), the keyboard body/backdrop (`keyboard_surface`, `keyboard_surface_dim`), and the surrounding app chrome via the standard Material 3 roles (`surface`, five `surface_container*` elevations, `background`, `outline`, `outline_variant`, `scrim`, `inverse_*`, `error*`) - which is how settings screens, the theme picker, clipboard and emoji panels get themed by the same file. The Compose-rendered action/suggestion bar is covered and gets its OWN opacity control (`action_bar_opacity`, default 0.5) separate from the key area. Key-preview popups and long-press mini-keyboards are themed: `keyPreviewBackground`, `keyPreviewOffset`, `keyPreviewHeight`, `moreKeysKeyboardLayout` in attrs.xml, plus KeyPreviewChoreographer / KeyPreviewDrawParams / KeyPreviewView for animation timing; a match rule can additionally target keys via the 'in popup' qualifier so mini-keyboard keys can be styled differently from the main grid. Spacebar has dedicated attributes (`spacebarBackground`, `languageOnSpacebarTextColor`, `languageOnSpacebarTextRatio`). Gesture trail is themed via MainKeyboardView assets. [uncertain] - system NAVIGATION BAR color: HeliBoard has an explicit NAVIGATION_BAR token and FUTO does not appear to expose one by that name; I could not confirm whether the nav bar is tinted implicitly from keyboard_surface.
sound_haptic_theming: Not themed. There are no sound or haptic fields anywhere in SerializedTomlFile - no `[sound]` or `[haptics]` section, no audio asset type in `[asset]`, and the theme zip carries only images plus shader/color data. Key sound and vibration remain global user settings driven by standard Android APIs (AudioManager keypress FX and Vibrator / HapticFeedbackConstants), independent of which theme is active. Practical implication for anyone copying this design: FUTO deliberately scoped 'theme' to visuals only, so a commercial keyboard wanting sound packs is adding a dimension the format has no slot for and would need a parallel manifest section plus an audio asset type.
platform_apis_frameworks: Android only. InputMethodService (subclassed as `InputMethodServiceCompose`) + AOSP LatinIME's Canvas-drawn KeyboardView/MainKeyboardView; Android Drawable / StateListDrawable / ColorFilter for key art; Jetpack Compose + Jetpack Navigation for the action bar, settings and background composable; Jetpack DataStore plus SharedPreferences for settings (KeyBordersSetting, HiddenKeysSetting, KeyHintsSetting); Material 3 color science (Hct, TonalPalette, DynamicScheme VIBRANT) and Android 12+ Material You dynamic color; EGL + OpenGL ES 2.0 context running GLSL ES 3.2 fragment shaders with FBO render-to-texture for animated backgrounds - notably NOT Android 13's RuntimeShader/AGSL; raw GLES was chosen, which keeps minSdk low; java.util.zip.ZipFile for theme packages; kotlinx-serialization for JSON plus a TOML parser for theme.txt; XML attrs.xml styleables (KeyboardTheme, KeyboardView, MainKeyboardView, Keyboard_Key) for the built-in static themes, with themes-*.xml providing a cascade (KeyboardTheme.LXX_Light -> KeyboardView.LXX_Light -> MainKeyboardView.LXX_Light).
delivery_installation_pipeline: Three coexisting channels, modeled by `ThemeOption`, described in source as 'a sealed class representing different theme sources (Presets, Custom, Dynamic)'. (1) BUNDLED: preset themes shipped in the APK under theme/presets/. (2) DYNAMIC: Material You palette pulled live from the OS - no file at all. (3) CUSTOM / SIDELOADED: a `.zip` produced either by the in-app simple editor or the desktop web editor at https://keyboard.futo.tech/theme-editor, shared 'anywhere' (no store, no signing, no account) and imported through the app's theme menu. On import the zip is copied WHOLE into `context.filesDir/themes/` - app-private internal storage, one zip per theme, keyed by id (>= 3 chars, must not end in `_`). Assets are NOT unpacked to disk: `ZipThemes.loadFile()` opens a `ZipFile` and hands the engine a ThemeDecodingContext whose `getFileBytes(path)` pulls entries on demand and whose `close()` closes the zip - so the on-disk footprint stays compressed and there is no extracted-asset directory to manage, garbage-collect or secure. A first-party gallery exists at https://keyboard.futo.tech/themes with stated plans to accept user submissions. Delivery is fully offline-capable; nothing requires network permission at type time.
permission_store_policy_surface: Android, so no iOS-style Full Access analogue exists. Importing a theme is a user-initiated file pick (SAF), so no storage permission is required, and the keyboard itself needs no INTERNET permission to apply themes. Because themes are plain zips sideloaded by the user rather than downloadable executable code, this design sidesteps the Google Play problems that killed the legacy 'theme plugin APK' pattern (one installable APK per theme) - a model FUTO explicitly does not use. FUTO's own distribution is off-Play (direct APK / their own channels), so Play review pressure on theme content is largely moot upstream. BUT anyone copying this design into a Play-distributed app should note that a first-party gallery serving user-submitted zips makes the app a UGC host under Play's User Generated Content policy (moderation and in-app reporting obligations), even though the payload is only images and shader text. [uncertain] - no published FUTO moderation policy for the themes gallery was found. Licensing: the GitHub repo is a mirror of gitlab.futo.org and FUTO generally ships under its 'Source First' licensing rather than a classic OSI license; the LatinIME base is Apache-2.0. Treat the theming module as readable-for-reference, not as freely reusable. [uncertain] on the exact license covering the theming code.
memory_performance_budget: No hard platform ceiling - Android IMEs get a normal app heap, unlike iOS's ~40-60MB extension cap - and the code reflects that relaxed posture, which is the main thing NOT to copy. Mitigations that ARE present and worth stealing: the shader background renders into an offscreen FBO at `renderRes = 256 to 256` and is upscaled to keyboard bounds via a copy shader, so animated-background fill cost is FIXED at 64k pixels regardless of screen size or device density; `iTime` wraps at 120,000 ms to avoid float precision drift in long-running shaders; textures use GL_LINEAR / GL_REPEAT; asset bytes are read lazily from the still-open zip rather than decoded up front; and thumbnails avoid a full theme load via `loadSchemeThumb()`, which wraps the decoding context so only the thumbnailImage entry resolves (`if (path == i.second.thumbnailImage) i.first.getFileBytes(path) else null`) and everything else returns null. Weaknesses: three caches - `themeCache: MutableMap<ThemeFileName, KeyboardColorScheme>`, `thumbThemeCache`, and `bitmapCache: MutableMap<String, ImageBitmap>` - have NO size limit and NO eviction policy; they grow unbounded and are cleared only by explicit `invalidateCache(name)` on save/import/delete. There is no documented max decoded bitmap dimension and no downsampling of the user's background photo before decode (`target_density = 640.0` scales borders and icons, not the background), so a large source image is decoded at full size. Animation is permitted and unthrottled beyond the 256x256 render size. For a memory-constrained port (especially iOS) the transferable ideas are the fixed-resolution offscreen render and the thumbnail-only decoding context; the unbounded caches are a liability to fix, not to copy.
untrusted_theme_validation_security: The weakest area, and worth reading as a cautionary example. ZIP HANDLING: entries are pulled by name through `zipFile.getEntry(path)` rather than by iterating and extracting to a directory - since nothing is written to disk under an attacker-controlled name, classic ZIP-SLIP path traversal is structurally avoided, but there is no explicit path sanitization in the code. MANIFEST HANDLING: TomlZipTheme configs are checked with `if (!cfg.validate()) throw Exception("Validation failed")`, BUT that exception is caught and the failure is only accumulated into the `errors: String` field on SerializableTheme - import then PROCEEDS. So a theme failing the 0.08 luminance-difference contrast check, or otherwise malformed, still installs; validation is advisory, not blocking. Weak ID hygiene exists (length >= 3, no trailing underscore) and deletion is restricted to custom (non-bundled) themes. IMAGE DECODING: no documented dimension cap, no decode-bounds pre-pass, and base64 `data:` URIs are decoded straight from the manifest - a decompression bomb or oversized-bitmap OOM is not defended against. SHADER CONTENT: arbitrary user GLSL is compiled and run on the GPU, a real if low-severity attack surface - a pathological shader can hang or GPU-DoS the IME. Anyone shipping downloadable themes commercially should add: decode-bounds sampling with a hard max bitmap dimension, a zip entry-count and uncompressed-size cap, a shader compile/instruction budget with timeout, and BLOCKING manifest validation.
open_source_reference_availability: Yes - readable, and the single best public reference for 'background image done properly'. GitHub mirror: https://github.com/futo-org/android-keyboard (canonical: https://gitlab.futo.org/keyboard/latinime). The theming module is one directory: `java/src/org/futo/inputmethod/latin/uix/theme/` - Theme.kt, ThemeOptions.kt, AdvancedThemeOptions.kt, AdvancedThemeCustomizer.kt, CustomThemeBuilder.kt, KeyedBitmaps.kt (the match-rule engine), ShaderRenderer.kt, ZipThemes.kt, ThemeDecodingContext.kt, decodeUtils.kt, Type.kt, plus subpackages presets/, selector/, serialization/ (Common.kt, Json.kt, Toml.kt). Static XML themes live in java/res/values/attrs.xml and themes-*.xml. Generated architecture docs: https://deepwiki.com/futo-org/android-keyboard/3.3-themes-and-styling. Design rationale thread: https://github.com/futo-org/android-keyboard/issues/1719. CAVEAT: source-AVAILABLE under FUTO's licensing rather than plainly OSI-licensed - study it, do not paste it. [uncertain] on the precise license applying to the theming module.
authoring_tooling_preview_generation: Two-tier tooling, deliberately split by DEVICE - a pattern worth copying. SIMPLE editor: in-app, on-phone, for end users - pick a photo, crop it, set transparency/blur, light vs dark, key borders on/off, and the palette is auto-derived from the image. ADVANCED editor: a WEB editor at https://keyboard.futo.tech/theme-editor, explicitly desktop-only ('advanced theming by artists or developers is done via a new web editor with a desktop device'), exposing all 44 colors, match rules and bitmap border/icon assets, and exporting the `.zip`. Scoping phone authoring to the simple tier is an intentional UX decision, not a limitation. PREVIEW/THUMBNAIL: the manifest carries a dedicated `thumbnailImage` field (part of the SerializableTheme interface) - the AUTHOR supplies the preview image rather than the app rendering one, and `loadSchemeThumb()` loads ONLY that entry so the theme picker renders a grid without decoding every theme's full asset set. That is a concrete, cheap answer to store-thumbnail generation. Distribution gallery: https://keyboard.futo.tech/themes. Shipping history: v0.1.27 (2024-12-25) introduced simple theming; v0.1.30-rc1 (2025-07-28) introduced advanced theming, the web editor and the gallery.
cross_platform_token_parity: No cross-platform story - FUTO Keyboard is Android-only and the format is Android-bound in several places. PORTABLE parts: the 44 color tokens (Material 3 role names, which map onto any design system), `roundedness`, `scale_text` / `scale_hints`, `weight_text` / `weight_hints`, the normalized `cropping` rect, the two opacity values, the `thumbnailImage` convention, and the abstract selector->asset match-rule idea. INHERENTLY PLATFORM-BOUND: `background: Drawable` and the whole Drawable/ColorFilter key-art model; GLSL ES fragment shaders driven through EGL/OpenGL ES 2.0 (an iOS port would need Metal, Core Image or SwiftUI equivalents and shader source would not transfer verbatim); `target_density = 640.0` assumes Android density buckets; the KeyVisualStyle / backgroundType role enum comes from AOSP LatinIME; Material You extraction has no iOS analogue. Verdict: the MANIFEST is a good cross-platform template; the RENDERER is not.
animation_budget: Animated themes ARE supported, but ONLY through the shader path - there is no Lottie, GIF or video field anywhere in the manifest. `AdvancedThemeOptions.backgroundShader: String?` holds GLSL source; ShaderRenderer drives it with `iTime` (seconds, wrapping every 120s / 120,000 ms) on an EGL + OpenGL ES 2.0 context, rendering to a 256x256 FBO that is upscaled - so the effective cost cap is the FIXED RENDER RESOLUTION rather than a frame-rate cap. Key-press animation is separate and non-theme (KeyPreviewChoreographer timings from XML), and FlickClipDrawable animates directional flick highlights. OPEN / WEAKLY DOCUMENTED QUESTION [uncertain]: I found no documented frame-rate cap, no documented pause-when-idle or pause-on-onFinishInputView behavior, and no battery-impact guidance in the sources I could reach. Since an IME is visible only while typing this may be acceptable in practice, but if you copy this design, an explicit 'stop the GL loop when the input view is hidden' rule and a 30/60fps cap are things you would have to add yourself - they are not evidenced in the source or docs.
key_takeaways_for_mochi: Most transferable idea: put a DynamicThemeProvider-style interface between the views and the palette source, so 'static preset', 'OS dynamic color' and 'user-downloaded theme' are three implementations of one interface and no view knows the difference.

Hybrid is the right rendering answer for background images: one whole-surface background layer plus a real per-key layer, with the scrim folded into computed key-container alpha rather than drawn as a separate rectangle. (1 - opacity^2) * 0.32 + 0.5 is a usable starting formula.
Normalized crop rects ([0,0,1,1] fractions, not pixels) are what let one background image survive variable keyboard height, rotation and tablets.
Selector -> asset match rules keyed on ROLE, key code and ASPECT-RATIO BUCKET (not row/col indices) are what let theme art survive layout, locale and number-row changes.
Author-supplied thumbnailImage plus a decoding context that resolves only that entry gives a cheap theme-picker grid without decoding every theme.
Reading the zip in place (ZipFile + on-demand getFileBytes) instead of extracting to disk avoids an entire class of path-traversal and cleanup problems.
Copy the format, not the safety posture: unbounded caches, advisory-only validation and no bitmap size cap are things FUTO gets away with on Android that would sink an iOS keyboard extension.
